meta.subtitle: Aerospace and defense prime; Q2'26 sales $24.7B up 14%, backlog $289B, guide raised; FY25 net debt $30.5B at 2.0x EBITDA

analystSentiment.commentary: RTX reported Q2'26 results on July 23, 2026: sales of $24.7B, {+ up 14% +} year over year and up 16% organically, adjusted EPS of $1.89, {+ up 21% +}, and a backlog of $289B, {+ up 22% +} year over year. Management raised its 2026 outlook to adjusted EPS of $7.10-$7.25 and free cash flow of $8.50-$8.75B. The balance sheet carries FY25 net debt of $30.5B, 2.0x trailing EBITDA. At $193.12 on September 23, 2026, the shares trade at 34.0x trailing earnings, 26.7x forward earnings and 19.4x EV/EBITDA. We rate RTX HOLD with a $190-$230 target range. The operating story is strong, and the price already reflects most of it. Holding today's forward multiple as the year rolls onto FY27E EPS of $7.85 gives our $210 Base case, only modestly above the price, while a Bear case that prices a cost shock to both earnings and the multiple sits at $150. The weighted fair value of $205.50 gives expected upside of +6.4% against bear-case downside of -22.3%, short of the desk's BUY bar. The deciding input is how the Base case is anchored, which the valuation section argues from both sides.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: RTX Corporation is an aerospace and defense company serving commercial, military and government customers worldwide. It operates through three segments: Collins Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney and Raytheon. Collins Aerospace supplies aerospace and defense products and aftermarket services, including power, environmental, flight-control and cabin systems for civil and military aircraft. Pratt & Whitney supplies aircraft engines for commercial, military, business-jet and general-aviation customers, along with auxiliary power units and aftermarket maintenance, repair and overhaul services. Raytheon provides threat detection, tracking and mitigation capabilities, including sensors and mission systems, for government and commercial customers. Raytheon follows a fiscal calendar, so its Q2'26 ended June 28, 2026, while Collins and Pratt & Whitney use calendar quarter ends. The company was formerly known as Raytheon Technologies Corporation and changed its name to RTX Corporation in July 2023. RTX was incorporated in 1934 and is headquartered in Arlington, Virginia, with more than 180,000 employees and 2025 sales of more than $88 billion.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: RTX pairs a large installed base of engines and aircraft systems with a defense business exposed to munitions and missile-defense demand. Q2'26 margins widened in all three segments, and management raised its 2026 outlook for adjusted sales, adjusted EPS and free cash flow. We like the business and the visibility its backlog gives. We do not see enough upside at $193.12. The shares trade at 26.7x forward earnings and 19.4x EV/EBITDA, with net debt at 2.0x EBITDA, so the next year's return rests on earnings growth rather than a re-rating. The Powder Metal Matter, tariffs and fixed-price cost pressure give the downside more room than the upside. Execution to the guide earns roughly our Base case, which is why we rate the shares HOLD rather than BUY.

catalysts: Backlog conversion: the $289B backlog at the end of Q2'26, split $170B commercial and $119B defense, supports the raised 2026 outlook as programs ship.

Defense budget requests: the proposed $1.5 trillion FY2027 defense budget, released April 21, 2026, and a June 24, 2026 supplemental request that includes $21 billion for munitions replenishment could add demand for RTX munitions if Congress funds them.

Golden Dome and munitions funding: the July 4, 2025 Act provides $24.4 billion for the Golden Dome for America project and $25.4 billion for munitions and supply chain resiliency; the MD&A says any material impact will depend on actual awards, award timelines, mission priorities and future budget determinations.
Segment margins: Q2'26 return on sales rose at Collins Aerospace, Pratt & Whitney and Raytheon, and holding those gains through the second half would support the top of the raised outlook.

Tariff refunds: RTX has paid approximately $0.5 billion of IEEPA tariffs and has submitted refund claims; it will recognize refunds if and when approved, and the U.S. government appealed the refund order on June 2, 2026.
risks: Valuation: the trailing and forward earnings multiples leave little room for a miss; the valuation section sets out the numbers.
Leverage: FY25 net debt of $30.5B stands ahead of the equity; the balance-sheet discussion covers what it means for the downside.
Powder Metal Matter: Pratt & Whitney's 2023 finding requires accelerated inspection of the PW1100 GTF fleet that powers the A320neo family.
Capital-return policy: an executive order may limit distributions and share repurchases during periods of defense-contractor underperformance.
Tariffs and supply chain: new tariff regimes may apply to RTX's imports, and the company expects supply-chain disruptions to continue.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.incomeCommentary: Revenue grew from $64.4B in FY21 to $88.6B in FY25, {+ up 9.7% +} in the latest year after {+ 17.1% +} growth in FY24. Operating margin rose from 8.0% in FY21 to 10.5% in FY25, after a trough of 5.2% in FY23 that the excerpts here do not explain. FY25 operating income was $9.3B, net income $6.7B and diluted EPS $4.96. Q2'26 sales were $24.7B; the press release puts growth at 14% year over year and the vendor's quarterly data at 14.5%, and we use the company's 14%. The Q2'26 operating margin was 11.4%, against 11.2% on the trailing twelve months, and the trailing net margin was 8.3%. GAAP EPS was $1.57, {+ up 29% +} from $1.22, and included $0.27 of acquisition accounting adjustments; adjusted EPS was $1.89, {+ up 21% +}. The company credits the growth in adjusted net income to higher adjusted segment operating profit in all three segments. Pratt & Whitney's reported operating profit rose 50%, but the prior-year quarter included an approximately $100 million charge related to a customer bankruptcy, so its adjusted rise of 22% is the cleaner measure. The recovery since FY23 is real, but no year before FY25 in the series had an operating margin above 8.2%, so the multiple depends on RTX holding the higher level for another year.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.balanceCommentary: RTX ended FY25 with total debt of $37.9B, cash and short-term investments of $8.2B and net debt of $30.5B, against total equity of $67.1B. Debt rose from $31.9B in FY22 to $43.8B in FY23, the year RTX also bought back $12.9B of stock, and has fallen in each year since, to $41.3B in FY24 and the FY25 level above. Net debt followed, down from $37.2B in FY23. The March 9, 2026 proxy statement credits the CFO with paying down $3.4 billion of debt in 2025. On the trailing twelve months, net debt is 2.0x EBITDA, and FY25 EBITDA was $13.7B. That is moderate leverage for a company with positive free cash flow in each of the past five years, and the direction is down. Two points temper the read. The MD&A says higher interest rates have increased the cost of borrowing and tightened the availability of capital. And net debt is a fixed claim ahead of shareholders, so any fall in enterprise value takes a somewhat larger share of the equity value; the 19.4x EV/EBITDA multiple is the one that captures this. Liquidity is tight but stable: the current ratio was 1.03 at FY25 and 1.01 on the trailing twelve months, within the 0.99 to 1.19 range of the past five years. The balance sheet does not threaten the thesis, but at that ratio it is not a cushion either, and further paydown is the use of cash that most directly lowers the risk to the equity.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December 31.

financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation improved in FY25: operating cash flow was $10.6B, capital expenditure -$2.6B and free cash flow $7.9B, a 9.0% free-cash-flow margin, above the 5.6% to 7.9% range of FY21 to FY24. FY25 free cash flow covered dividends paid of -$3.6B, and share repurchases were only -$0.1B, which left room for the debt reduction described under the balance sheet. Q2'26 free cash flow was {+ $2.9B +}, up from {- -$72 million -} a year earlier, on operating cash flow of $3.5B against $458 million and capital expenditure of $0.7B. Because the prior-year quarter was negative, the year-over-year swing flatters the comparison. Management's raised 2026 free-cash-flow outlook of $8.50-$8.75B is the better gauge of the run rate, and it sits above the FY25 level. The trailing free-cash-flow yield is 4.4%.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: At $193.12, RTX trades at 34.0x trailing earnings, 2.8x sales and 19.4x EV/EBITDA, and the trailing free-cash-flow yield is 4.4%. EV/EBITDA includes the FY25 net debt, so it is the multiple that reflects the whole capital structure. The vendor labels its 26.7x forward multiple next-twelve-month, but at today's price it lines up with consensus FY26E EPS of $7.24, so we treat it as a current-year multiple; on FY27E EPS of $7.85 the multiple is about 24.6x. Consensus FY26E EPS sits inside the company's adjusted EPS outlook of $7.10-$7.25, which suggests it is struck on the adjusted basis. The trailing multiple is on GAAP EPS, which in Q2'26 included $0.27 of acquisition accounting adjustments, so part of the step-down from trailing to forward may be a difference in basis rather than growth. The pack carries no peer multiples, so this is an absolute read. The 23 analysts covering RTX rate it 15 Buy, 8 Hold and 0 Sell, with a consensus target of $234.41, a median of $240.00 and a range of $200.00 to $265.00. On these multiples the raised outlook is already in the price, and returns from here depend on earnings rather than on the multiple.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Execution runs ahead of the raised outlook: the Q2'26 trends carry through the second half, FY27E EPS of $7.85 proves too low, budget and supplemental requests turn into munitions awards, and the multiple on FY27E earnings expands well above today's 24.6x. The price lands at the Street median target of $240.00.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: RTX delivers the raised 2026 outlook and consensus FY27E EPS, and the 26.7x multiple the shares carry on current-year earnings today holds as the year rolls forward onto FY27E. Returns track earnings growth, with no re-rating.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: A cost shock: the Powder Metal Matter, tariffs and fixed-price overruns pull EPS back to the original 2026 outlook of $6.70-$6.90, and the forward multiple compresses to the low twenties. With net debt ahead of the equity, the share price falls below the 52-week low of $155.64.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: We weight the Base case at 55%, the Bull at 25% and the Bear at 20%. The weighted values are $60.00, $115.50 and $30.00, for a weighted fair value of $205.50, expected upside of +6.4%, bear-case downside of -22.3% and reward/risk of 0.29x. That derives HOLD, and HOLD is our label. The Bear weight rests on its own story: the Powder Metal Matter and the fixed-price exposure are live, but Q2'26 margins rose in every segment and the outlook went up, so a fall back to the original outlook is a real but minority outcome. Weights alone do not decide the label; only a Bull weight near one half would derive BUY. The anchor for the Base case does, and we call it a judgment. The case for a higher Base is the Street's: even its lowest target sits above the current price, the consensus target sits well above our Base, and the backlog growth supports further raises. With the Base set at the consensus target and the same weights, the scenarios would derive BUY. The case against is that reaching the consensus target within a year needs the multiple to expand from today's level while net debt is 2.0x EBITDA and consensus FY26E EPS already sits near the top of the raised outlook. We hold the multiple rather than expand it. Our $190-$230 target range brackets the $210 Base case.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The vendor feed reports RTX as a single consolidated line, but the company runs three operating segments, and the Q2'26 press release gives their results. Collins Aerospace sales were $8,210 million, up 8%, at a 15.9% reported return on sales, with commercial OE up 26% and commercial aftermarket up 10%. Pratt & Whitney sales were $8,889 million, up 16%, at an 8.3% return on sales, with commercial aftermarket up 25% and military up 23%, partly offset by lower commercial OE sales. Raytheon sales were $8,269 million, up 18%, at a 12.6% return on sales, on higher volume on land and air defense systems, naval programs, and air and space defense systems, including Patriot, Standard Missile and AMRAAM. All growth rates are year over year.

moatFactors.name: Aftermarket installed base
moatFactors.body: Many of RTX's aerospace customers are covered by long-term aftermarket service agreements at Collins and Pratt & Whitney, inclusive of spare parts and services. Q2'26 commercial aftermarket sales grew at double-digit rates at both businesses, as the segment detail shows, a recurring stream tied to an installed fleet that is hard for another supplier to displace.

moatFactors.name: Defense incumbency and backlog
moatFactors.body: RTX serves defense customers as a prime contractor or subcontractor on a broad portfolio of programs, with $119B of defense backlog at the end of Q2'26. Multi-year missile programs such as Patriot, Standard Missile and AMRAAM give visibility, though the government can terminate contracts for convenience.

moatFactors.name: Certification and technology barriers
moatFactors.body: Aircraft engines and defense systems demand certification, qualification and proven performance, which raises barriers to entry. The same demands cut both ways: untested technologies and fixed-price development contracts carry cost-overrun and performance risk that RTX bears.

moatFactors.name: Scale and diversification
moatFactors.body: More than 180,000 employees and 2025 sales of more than $88 billion across three segments and commercial and defense end markets give RTX scale and a mix that softens a shock to any single program.

businessMoat.durability: The moat rests on the installed base of engines and aircraft systems that generates long-term aftermarket revenue, and on defense incumbency backed by multi-year programs. Both are durable: aftermarket agreements run for years, and the MD&A describes the defense contracts to design, develop and manufacture complex equipment as long-cycle. The threats to durability are execution and policy rather than displacement. The Powder Metal Matter shows how a quality issue can force accelerated inspections, fixed-price development contracts can produce cost overruns, and the company says it cannot always pass cost increases through on fixed-price contracts. The franchise is wide, but the returns it earns depend on disciplined program execution.

points: Backlog conversion is the growth engine: the commercial and defense backlog ships over multi-year aftermarket and program cycles and underpins the raised organic-growth outlook.
Management lifted its 2026 outlook on July 23, 2026: adjusted sales to $95.0-$96.0B from $92.5-$93.5B, organic growth to 8-9% from 5-6%, and adjusted EPS to $7.10-$7.25 from $6.70-$6.90.
Q2'26 organic sales grew 16% year over year, ahead of the full-year organic outlook, led by double-digit commercial aftermarket and defense growth.
Consensus puts FY26E revenue at $96.1B and FY27E at $103.2B, with EPS of $7.24 and $7.85, which implies slower growth in FY27 than in FY26.

Defense funding reaches RTX through munitions replenishment and missile-defense work, and the MD&A says RTX is strategically situated to support the munitions initiative; awards, timing and appropriations decide how much of it becomes revenue.

management.leadership: According to the July 23, 2026 press release, RTX is led by Chairman and CEO Chris Calio, who described Q2'26 as 16% organic growth with margin expansion in all three segments. The March 9, 2026 proxy statement names Neil G. Mitchill, Jr. as Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, with 11 years at RTX; Philip J. Jasper as President, Raytheon, with 34 years; and Shane G. Eddy as President, Pratt & Whitney, with 16 years. Management's stated priorities are executing on the backlog, increasing productivity, expanding capacity and introducing new technologies. The proxy says the CFO oversaw 2025 results that exceeded the adjusted net sales, adjusted EPS and free-cash-flow expectations communicated to investors, despite tariff and supplier headwinds. The 2025 record and the Q2'26 raise support confidence in execution.
management.capitalAllocation: Since FY23, capital allocation has favored debt reduction and dividends over buybacks. Share repurchases fell from $12.9B in FY23 to $0.4B in FY24 and $0.1B in FY25, while the deleveraging described under the balance sheet proceeded. The proxy says that in 2025 RTX invested $7.7 billion in company- and customer-funded research and development and capital expenditures, increased its annual dividend rate by 7.9% and returned over $3.6 billion of capital to shareowners. The quarterly dividend rose from $0.63 to $0.68 per share in the second quarter of 2025, and the current dividend yield is 1.53%. At 2.0x net debt to EBITDA, we think paydown ahead of buybacks is the right order. One policy constraint applies: an executive order may limit distributions and share repurchases during periods of defense-contractor underperformance, and the company warns that such a limit could adversely affect the share price.
management.governance: Governance rests on the DEF 14A proxy statement dated March 9, 2026. Under RTX's Director Independence Policy and NYSE listing standards, a majority of directors must be independent; the Board determined that, other than Mr. Calio as a current RTX employee, each nominee for the 2026 Annual Meeting satisfies the independence criteria. Directors complete an annual questionnaire on relationships and transactions that may affect independence. Related-person transactions above $120,000 require Governance Committee review. On pay, the HCC Committee approved a 164% of target performance factor for Corporate and a $7.5 million 2026 LTI award for the CFO, an amount above the market median for his role. The structure is conventional and the board is independent apart from the CEO; above-median awards in a year of above-expectation results do not concern us. The MD&A adds that the Russian government has imposed counter-sanctions targeting certain members of RTX's management team and Board of Directors.

idiosyncratic: Pratt & Whitney Powder Metal Matter: in 2023 Pratt & Whitney determined that a rare condition in powder metal used to manufacture certain engine parts requires accelerated inspection of the PW1100 GTF fleet that powers the A320neo family. The excerpts carry no cost estimate, so the size of any further charge is unknown.

Fixed-price contract exposure: under firm fixed-price contracts RTX carries the burden of cost overruns, and under fixed-price incentive contracts it carries all overruns above the ceiling price; inflation, tariffs and supply constraints could produce losses it cannot always offset through pricing.

Tariffs: refunds of the IEEPA tariffs RTX paid depend on the outcome of the U.S. government's appeal, and new and revised tariffs imposed after the Supreme Court ruling may apply to products RTX imports.

Capital-return limits: an executive order may limit distributions, share repurchases and executive compensation incentives during periods of defense-contractor underperformance under U.S. government contracts.
Program execution: contract terminations for convenience or default, performance delays and cost overruns on advanced programs could impair results and future award opportunities.
risks.systemic: Systemic risk centers on U.S. government defense spending and the macro environment. U.S. government sales are a significant portion of consolidated sales, and budget changes, continuing resolutions or shutdowns could delay awards, payments and new program starts. The MD&A cites inflation, interest rates, foreign-currency movements and volatile global trade policy as sources of uncertainty for cost and demand. The global supply chain remains constrained, and management expects disruptions to continue, affecting raw materials including certain rare earth elements, microelectronics and certain commodities. Commercial aerospace demand is tied to revenue passenger miles, the financial health of airlines and the performance of airframers, so a downturn in air travel would weigh on Collins and Pratt & Whitney. These factors sit largely outside the company's control and inform the Bear weight.

body: We rate RTX HOLD with a target range of $190 to $230 against the $193.12 price of September 23, 2026. The business is executing well, and the raised outlook and backlog support our $210 Base case. At 26.7x forward earnings and 19.4x EV/EBITDA, with net debt at 2.0x EBITDA, the shares already price that execution: the weighted fair value of $205.50 leaves expected upside of +6.4% against bear-case downside of -22.3%.

The label is more sensitive to the price than to the weights, and in that sense the call is close. On these scenarios, a pullback of a few percent from today's price would derive BUY, because the upside and reward/risk tests both clear just below today's price, and a price modestly above our Base case would derive SELL. The page's price history shows a steady decline over the six weeks to September 23 from closes near the 52-week high, and no source in the pack explains it; on these scenarios the mid-August closes would have derived SELL and the early-September closes HOLD. On the evidence, we would raise the Base case if the company lifts its 2026 outlook again or consensus FY27E EPS moves above $7.85 while the price lags. We would move weight to the Bear case if segment margins give back the Q2'26 gains or the outlook is cut.
